result:
I keep coming back to inventories. Not lists of things to do — those are anxious documents — but catalogs of what exists. Seed catalogs from 1890 with three hundred varieties of apple, most of them extinct now: Sops of Wine, Westfield Seek-No-Further, Maiden's Blush. Ship manifests. The Domesday Book, which was essentially William the Conqueror asking, with menace, *what have we got?* Sears Roebuck mailing a thousand pages of hardware to farmhouses.

What draws me is that an inventory is an argument dressed as a neutral document. Someone decided what counted as a thing. Someone decided the apple was worth a line and the weeds in the orchard weren't. The categories leak. There's always a final entry that reads "sundries" or "other," which is where the actual world gets swept.

I like that the impulse to catalog is both imperial and tender. It's how you tax a village and also how you remember your grandmother's china pattern. The census-taker and the person labeling boxes after a death are performing nearly identical operations with opposite tempers.

And inventories always fail interestingly. They're snapshots of a thing that won't hold still. The apple varieties were vanishing even as they were printed — the catalog is simultaneously the proudest record and the death certificate. You can read the 1890 list as an achievement or as a loss report, depending on the decade you're standing in.

Which makes me think the honest inventory would have to include a column for *rate of disappearance.* Nobody does this. Understandably. But it would be the most accurate document ever produced, and unbearable to consult.
